newsitem.title: USA: Jimmy Stewart's hometown saddened by actor's death.
newsitem.headline: Jimmy Stewart's hometown saddened by actor's death.

text.p: Residents of the rural western Pennsylvania town, population 15,000, where actor Jimmy Stewart was born said Wednesday his death will leave "a big void" in the town.

A statue of the actor, whose father once owned a hardware store there, stands in front of the courthouse and six years ago the town opened a Jimmy Stewart museum containing costumes and memorabilia from his 83 films.
Each year since then the museum has held a festival to recall "It's A Wonderful Life," the 1946 film that has become a Christmas classic in which Stewart starred as George Bailey.

Cast members from the film visiting there last year told the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette that Indiana, which calls itself "the Christmas tree capital of the world," resembles Bedford Falls, the town that Stewart saves in the film.
Stewart last visited Indiana, 45 miles northeast of Pittsburgh, 14 years ago, said Linda Moore Mack, the court clerk who was chairperson for his 75th birthday party celebration there in 1983.

Of Stewart's death, she said: "It's going to leave a big void. He was universally loved. He was a wonderful man and was devoted to his family and this country. He always cared about other people and how they felt."
Stewart died Wednesday from cardiac arrest at his home in Beverly Hills. He was 89.
Mack said Stewart attended his birthday celebration in Indiana with his late wife Gloria and she met the couple at that time.
Jay Rubin, president of the Jimmy Stewart Museum, said he also knew Stewart and had been a guest at his Beverly Hills home on several occasions.
"He was a great man," Rubin said. "He was a rare breed who was always sincere in what he said and in his actions. We're all very upset ... it's a sad day."
"He means a great deal to Indiana," Rubin said. "We're still absorbing the news of his death, but we're going to do something special to celebrate his life."

Stewart, born in Indiana on May 20, 1908, said he "grew up" in his father's hardware store, and after he won an Oscar for "The Philadelphia Story" in 1940 he sent it back to his father to display in the store.
A biography said he inherited his methodical trademark speech patterns from his partially deaf mother.
Although he studied architecture at Princeton, he pursued a career in acting after joining the University Players Group in Falmouth, Mass., where one of his fellow actors was Henry Fonda.
